The Authentication Debate That Never Ends
If you have spent any time in backend development or system design, you have almost certainly come across the debate between Session-Based Authentication and JSON Web Tokens (JWT). Modern applications often default to JWT because it is marketed as the scalable, stateless solution. Many developers believe that once an application reaches millions of users, sessions become a bottleneck while JWT naturally scales.
The reality is more nuanced. Scalability is not determined by whether authentication is stateful or stateless. Instead, it depends on how well your system handles security, operational complexity, and real world incidents. At a scale of 10 million users, authentication is no longer just about verifying identities. It is about maintaining control over millions of active sessions while responding immediately to security events. In that environment, I would choose Session-Based Authentication over JWT for most applications.
Why JWT Became So Popular
JWT gained popularity because it removes the need for the server to store session information. Instead of maintaining a session in memory or a database, the server generates a signed token containing user information and sends it to the client. Every subsequent request carries that token, allowing the server to verify the signature without performing a session lookup.
This stateless architecture provides several advantages. It reduces the dependency on centralized session storage, simplifies horizontal scaling, and allows different services to authenticate users without sharing a common session database. These characteristics make JWT particularly attractive in cloud native environments and distributed systems.
At first glance, it appears to be the perfect solution for applications expecting massive traffic.
The Hidden Cost of Stateless Authentication
The biggest weakness of JWT becomes apparent the moment something goes wrong.
Imagine a user’s account is compromised and an attacker obtains a valid JWT. Since the token is self contained and independently verifiable, it remains valid until its expiration time. The server cannot simply revoke it because the server is not maintaining any state about that token.
This creates a security window where an attacker can continue making authenticated requests even after the legitimate user changes their password or reports the account compromise.
For applications dealing with financial data, enterprise systems, healthcare platforms, or any security sensitive environment, waiting for token expiration is often unacceptable.
The Blocklist Problem
Developers often solve this issue by introducing a token blocklist.
Whenever a user logs out, changes their password, or has their account disabled, the corresponding JWT is added to a centralized blacklist. Every incoming request now checks whether the token exists in that blacklist before granting access.
While this approach works, it introduces an interesting contradiction.
The primary advantage of JWT is that it eliminates server side state. The moment a blocklist is introduced, the server once again depends on centralized state for every authenticated request.
In other words, the architecture gradually starts resembling traditional session management while retaining much of JWT’s operational complexity.
Why Sessions Provide Better Control
Session-Based Authentication follows a different approach.
Instead of storing authentication data inside the client, the server creates a session and stores it in a centralized session store. The client only receives a session identifier, usually stored inside a secure cookie.
Every request references that session, allowing the server to decide whether the session is still valid.
This design gives administrators complete control over authentication.
If a user’s account is compromised, the session can be deleted immediately.
If the user changes their password, every active session can be invalidated instantly.
If suspicious activity is detected, the server can terminate only the affected session without impacting other devices.
There is no waiting period and no dependency on token expiration.
Do Sessions Really Scale?
One of the oldest criticisms of Session-Based Authentication is scalability.
The argument suggests that maintaining millions of sessions requires excessive memory and prevents horizontal scaling because multiple application servers need access to the same session data.
This criticism was valid many years ago.
Today, distributed in memory data stores such as Redis have largely solved this challenge.
Redis is capable of storing millions of sessions while delivering extremely low latency lookups. Multiple application servers can access the same Redis cluster, making horizontal scaling straightforward without sacrificing centralized session management.
Large scale applications already rely on Redis for caching, rate limiting, queues, leaderboards, feature flags, and real time messaging. Maintaining session data within the same infrastructure is rarely the operational burden it once was.
At a scale of 10 million users, organizations are almost certainly operating distributed caching infrastructure already.
Operational Simplicity Matters
Authentication should not only be evaluated based on theoretical scalability. It should also be evaluated based on operational simplicity.
With sessions, user management becomes significantly easier.
Administrators can view every active login.
Users can sign out from all devices with a single operation.
Permissions can be updated immediately.
Compromised sessions can be revoked in seconds.
Security teams gain complete visibility into active user activity.
JWT, on the other hand, often requires additional mechanisms to achieve the same functionality. Token rotation, refresh tokens, revocation lists, and expiration strategies all increase implementation complexity.
What initially appears to be a lightweight authentication mechanism often grows into a much more sophisticated system as production requirements evolve.
When JWT Is the Better Choice
This does not mean JWT is a poor technology.
There are many scenarios where JWT is the ideal solution.
Distributed microservice architectures often benefit because multiple independent services can validate tokens without sharing a session database.
Third party APIs frequently use JWT because external clients cannot access an organization’s internal session infrastructure.
Mobile applications that communicate with multiple backend services also benefit from self contained authentication tokens.
In these environments, JWT provides flexibility that traditional sessions cannot easily match.
The key is choosing JWT because the architecture genuinely requires stateless authentication, not simply because it has become the industry trend.
Choosing the Right Tool
Authentication is ultimately a tradeoff between control and decentralization.
JWT reduces server side state but sacrifices immediate control over active authentication unless additional infrastructure is introduced.
Sessions require centralized storage but provide administrators with complete authority over every authenticated user.
At the scale of 10 million users, infrastructure capable of managing distributed sessions already exists. The cost of maintaining session state is relatively small compared to the operational advantages it provides.
Rather than chasing theoretical scalability, engineering teams should prioritize the ability to respond quickly when security incidents occur.
Final Thoughts
Technology decisions should always be driven by practical requirements rather than popularity.
JWT is an excellent solution for distributed systems, microservices, and third party authentication. However, for a single application serving millions of its own users, Session-Based Authentication often delivers a better balance of security, control, and operational simplicity.
Real world systems are rarely limited by authentication throughput alone. They are limited by how quickly they can adapt to failures, security threats, and changing user requirements.
At 10 million users, scalability is important. Control is even more important.
For that reason, I would rather manage session state than lose the ability to immediately revoke access when it matters most.
